title: What the Enemy Meant for Evil, God Meant for Good
paragraphs:
What the Enemy Meant for Evil, God Meant for Good
The Deeper Meaning of Genesis 50:20 and the Scandalous Grace That Rewrites Every Broken Story
There are verses in Scripture that comfort us.
There are verses that challenge us.
And then there are verses that completely rearrange the way we see our suffering.
Genesis 50:20 is one of those verses.
Not because it minimizes pain.
Not because it explains every tragedy.
But because it reveals something so breathtaking about God that many believers spend their entire lives trying to grasp its depth.
The verse says:
"As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today." (Genesis 50:20, ESV)
In Hebrew, the verse reads:
"אַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה"
"Atem chashavtem alai ra'ah; Elohim chashavah letovah."
Literally:
"You planned evil against me, but God planned it for good."
Notice carefully what the text does not say.
It does not say God merely reacted to evil.
It does not say God simply cleaned up the mess afterward.
It does not say God looked at a tragedy and attempted to salvage something useful.
The Hebrew word chashav means to devise, reckon, intend, weave, or purpose.
The brothers had intentions.
God had intentions.
Their intentions were wicked.
God's intentions were righteous.
The same event was moving through two different purposes simultaneously.
Human evil was real.
God's sovereignty was greater.
This is not a small theological detail.
This changes everything.
Because many people secretly believe that their worst moments permanently damaged God's plan for their lives.
The failed marriage.
The betrayal.
The addiction.
The abuse.
The years wasted in rebellion.
The scandal nobody knows about.
The decisions they would do anything to undo.
Many people carry a hidden fear that God can forgive them, but can never truly redeem what happened.
Joseph's story destroys that lie.
Joseph was not speaking from a place of theory.
He was speaking from scars.
His own brothers hated him.
They stripped him.
Humiliated him.
Threw him into a pit.
Sold him like property.
Allowed their father to believe he was dead.
Then came slavery.
False accusations.
Prison.
Years of isolation.
Years of confusion.
Years when God's promises appeared completely absent.
And yet when Joseph finally stood before the very men who had shattered his life, he did not deny their sin.
He did not pretend evil was good.
He did not rewrite history.
He named their evil honestly.
"You meant evil against me."
That is biblical truth.
Real forgiveness never requires pretending evil did not happen.
God never asks victims to call darkness light.
Sin is sin.
Evil is evil.
Betrayal is betrayal.
But Joseph saw something even bigger than the evil.
He saw God.
Not merely around the story.
Not merely after the story.
But throughout the story.
Working silently.
Patiently.
Sovereignly.
Redemptively.
While Joseph was in the pit, God was working.
While Joseph was in slavery, God was working.
While Joseph sat forgotten in prison, God was working.
While Joseph cried himself to sleep wondering where God was, God was working.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that.
Just because God feels silent does not mean He is absent.
Just because heaven seems quiet does not mean heaven is inactive.
Sometimes the deepest movements of God happen underground before anyone can see them.
The greatest miracle in Joseph's story was not becoming second-in-command of Egypt.
The greatest miracle was that suffering did not make him bitter.
Pain did not become his identity.
The pit did not become his future.
His wounds did not become his god.
Instead, grace transformed him.
And that points us to Someone greater.
Because Joseph's story is ultimately not about Joseph.
It is about Jesus.
The entire Bible points to Christ.
Joseph was betrayed by those closest to him.
Jesus was betrayed by one of His own disciples.
Joseph was sold for silver.
Jesus was sold for silver.
Joseph suffered although innocent.
Jesus suffered though completely sinless.
Joseph's suffering became the means of saving many lives.
Jesus' suffering became the means of saving the world.
The Greek New Testament tells us:
"Χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν" (1 Corinthians 15:3)
"Christ died for our sins."
At Calvary, humanity committed the greatest evil in history.
The Son of God was mocked.
Rejected.
Beaten.
Crucified.
The innocent Lamb was slaughtered.
Yet Acts 2:23 tells us that Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God.
The worst evil ever committed became the greatest act of redemption ever accomplished.
That is Genesis 50:20 on an eternal scale.
What humanity meant for evil.
God meant for good.
What looked like defeat became victory.
What looked like shame became salvation.
What looked like death became life.
And perhaps that is why Genesis 50:20 resonates so deeply with every human heart.
Because every one of us knows what it feels like to live inside a story that appears broken.
Some are carrying regret.
Some are carrying trauma.
Some are carrying guilt.
Some are carrying secret failures they pray nobody discovers.
Some are exhausted from asking why.
Why did this happen?
Why did they leave?
Why did God allow it?
Why did life unfold this way?
Genesis 50:20 does not answer every why.
But it reveals the Who.
The God who specializes in redemption.
The God who still writes final chapters.
The God who turns graves into gardens.
The God who brings beauty from ashes.
The God who transforms scandals into testimonies.
The God who takes the darkest pages and writes grace across them.
That does not mean every earthly story ends comfortably.
Joseph still carried scars.
Jesus still bears nail marks.
Redemption does not erase history.
Redemption transforms its meaning.
The cross did not disappear.
The cross became glorious.
Maybe your story feels like a pit right now.
Maybe it feels like a prison.
Maybe it feels like everything God promised is delayed.
Maybe you cannot see how anything good could possibly emerge from what happened.
Joseph could not see it either.
Not in the pit.
Not in slavery.
Not in prison.
Only later did he realize God had been writing a bigger story all along.
And perhaps years from now you will look back and discover that what felt like abandonment was actually preparation.
What felt like punishment was actually protection.
What felt like delay was actually divine timing.
What felt like an ending was only a chapter.
Because Jesus is still rewriting stories.
That is what grace does.
Grace walks into scandals.
Grace enters prisons.
Grace visits prodigals.
Grace restores failures.
Grace rescues sinners.
Grace rewrites everything.
If this message reached you at exactly the moment you needed it, don't keep it to yourself.
What part of your story are you still trusting God to redeem?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
If this ministry has blessed you, supporting it is one way to help more people encounter biblical truth and glorify God. Every share extends the reach. Every saved soul matters.
One day you may discover that the chapter you begged God to remove became the chapter He used to save someone else.
